title: Ahmad ibn Hanbal

lines: AN OLD MAN WITH AN INKWELL.
WITH THE INKWELL, TO THE GRAVE.
cards: An old man walks through Baghdad carrying an inkwell. Someone stops him. You've reached this rank, people call you an imam, and you still carry ink around like a student?
His answer, in a saying reported of him: with the inkwell, to the grave. That's Ahmad ibn Hanbal: old, honored, and still copying the reports line by line.
Today the Hanbali school begins, with a man who never stopped writing things down.

teach.h: A SCHOLAR WHO TRAVELED FOR REPORTS.
teach.b: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was a scholar of Baghdad, and above everything a scholar of hadith, the reports of what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said and did.
He traveled for them, his biographers say, to Kufa and Basra, to Mecca and Medina, and as far as Yemen, hearing reports from the people who carried them and writing them down.

He also studied with al-Shafi'i, and reports say each held the other in high regard. His method was his own. When a question came, he looked first to the Qur'an and the reports, then to what the Companions had said.

teach.h: A WEAK REPORT OVER A CLEVER ANALOGY.
teach.b: And reports say he would rather act on a weak hadith than on a jurist's analogy, as long as nothing stronger stood against it. Weak, here, doesn't mean made up. It means a chain of narrators with some doubt in it.

For him, a report with some doubt was still closer to the Prophet than a clever argument. Some early writers even listed him among the scholars of hadith rather than the jurists. His students saw it differently.
They wrote down his answers, one by one, about prayer, trade, marriage and manners, and out of those answers his school was built.
So his law is a law of answers: ask him something, and the reply might be a report, passed on rather than argued.

how: Hanbali scholars look first to the Qur'an and the hadith, then to the sayings of the Companions, and the school's rulings grew from Ahmad ibn Hanbal's recorded answers to questions.

o: a Baghdad scholar of hadith whose answers became a school
a caliph who questioned scholars about the Qur'an
a Medina scholar who wrote the well-trodden path

practice: Here's a short hadith, the one that opens Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are only by intentions, in Arabic innamal a'malu bin-niyyat.
Say it three times slowly, in whichever language sits easier, then once with your eyes closed, and ask what intention sits under the next thing you'll do today.
If you pray, you can ask that your intentions be good ones; if not, just keep the line on your tongue.

wordCard.voice: Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The scholar of Baghdad who traveled for hadith, put reports before reasoning, and whose answers became the Hanbali school. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the inkwell, from the saying reported of him: with the inkwell, to the grave.

carryVoice: Your line: the imam of hadith. The reports first, and the ink always close. Go gently.
